newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland bomb found as IRA urged to call truce.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland bomb found as IRA urged to call truce.

text.p: Security forces found a 1,000 pound (500 kilo) bomb near a British army base on Saturday and believe it was planted by IRA guerrillas to grab headlines in the run-up to British elections.
The device was found on the road between Clogh and Ballykinlar, site of a major British army base in County Down, south of Belfast.

It was left by the roadside in an apparently aborted attempt to blow up passing security force vehicles. An AK-47 assault rifle and detonating equipment were also found, police said. There was no immediate claim of responsibility but the attempt bore the hallmarks of the Irish Republican Army, which is fighting to end British rule and unite Northern Ireland with the Irish republic.
The IRA is ignoring appeals by the governments of Britain, Ireland and the United States to call a truce to get their political wing, Sinn Fein, into peace talks.
Britain's opposition Labour party, which could assume responsibility for troubled Northern Ireland if it wins a general election on May 1, repeated the call on Saturday.

Labour's spokeswoman on Northern Ireland, Mo Mowlam, told the British Broadcasting Corporation that, if the IRA called an immediate truce, Sinn Fein, its political wing, could take part in Belfast peace talks which resume on June 3.

She said such a truce would have to be called "pretty speedily" to allow time for the British government to verify that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) had ended all activities related to its war against British rule.
"If they show by word and deed that they are committed to the democratic process then we think they ought to safely move into the talks process," she said.

Mowlam's statement was seen signifying that there would be little change to Britain's Northern Ireland policy if Labour beats Prime Minister John Major's Conservative party, which is faring badly in national public opinion polls, in May.

Major's government says Sinn Fein, which seeks to reunite Northern Ireland with the Irish republic, is welcome to the talks once a verifiable IRA cease-fire is in place. The IRA has rejected any preconditions.

Mowlam said a British government would be satisfied that the cease-fire was genuine if targeting, surveillance and training ended and if there was a halt to IRA vigilante-style "punishment beatings" of minority Roman Catholics in the British province.

She was speaking the day after the IRA claimed responsibility for last Wednesday's twin bomb attacks on a railway network near Wilmslow in north-western England which severely disrupted traffic but caused no casualties.
The attack, the first in mainland Britain since last year, was seen as an attempt by IRA to put Northern Ireland on the British election agenda, where it gets scant attention.

The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year accusing the British government of placing impossible conditions on the entry of Sinn Fein into peace talks such as a commitment by the guerrillas to start disarming.
Pat Doherty, the Sinn Fein vice-president, told the BBC he welcomed Mowlam's remarks but he gave no hint of the likelihood of a new IRA truce.

Doherty said that he and party president Gerry Adams thought there could be a new IRA truce if the British government set a date for Sinn Fein's entry into peace talks with Protestant Unionists, who want the province to stay British.
